tags.title: Click letters: c, q, x
tags.description: In isiZulu orthography c, q and x (and combinations such as ch, gc, nc, qh, xh) write click consonants. Sesotho writes a click with q (for example 'qala'). In English these letters are never clicks: c in 'cat' is /k/, q in 'queen' is /kw/, x in 'six' is /ks/. A home-language reader may read the c in 'cat' as a click.
tags.teachingStrategy: Name the difference explicitly in the teaching language when c is introduced, contrast the click and /k/ in a listening task, and check with a 'which sound does c make here?' item whose distractor is the click.

tags.title: th and ph
tags.description: In isiZulu and Sesotho, 'th' and 'ph' write aspirated t and p (zu 'thatha', st 'thuto', zu 'phila', st 'phoofolo'). In English 'th' is /θ/ (thin) or /ð/ (the) and 'ph' is /f/ (phone). Learners may read 'the' with an aspirated t.
examples: zu: thatha, st: thuto (th = aspirated t)
tags.teachingStrategy: Teach 'the' as a sight word with an explicit note that English th is made with the tongue between the teeth; contrast with the home-language th.

tags.title: English short vowels
tags.description: English has more vowel sounds than isiZulu (5) or Sesotho (7, written with 5 letters). The short vowels in cat, pen, sit and bus have no exact home-language match: learners may read 'bus' with the home-language u (/u/) or merge 'pan' and 'pen'.
tags.teachingStrategy: Minimal-pair listening (which word did you hear?) before reading, slow model audio, and revision weighted to vowel errors.

tags.title: Short and long vowels (ship / sheep)
tags.description: English distinguishes words by vowel length and quality (ship / sheep, sit / seat). Vowel length is not used this way in isiZulu or Sesotho, so the difference can be hard to hear.
tags.teachingStrategy: Same-or-different listening tasks with clear model recordings; no reading demand until the sounds can be heard.

tags.title: Words that end in consonants
tags.description: isiZulu and Sesotho syllables almost always end in a vowel. English words often end in a consonant or a cluster (cat, desk, jobs). Learners may add a vowel ('cati') or drop the final sound.
tags.teachingStrategy: Point to the last letter during blending demonstrations, give 'listen to the last sound' feedback, and include final-sound distractors.

tags.title: Words that do not follow the sound rules
tags.description: isiZulu and Sesotho spelling is very regular. Many common English words are not (the, said, you, is), so sounding them out letter by letter does not work.
tags.teachingStrategy: Teach these as sight words: whole-word recognition, frequent revision, and an explicit explanation that English is less regular than the home language.

tags.title: Letter names and letter sounds
tags.description: English letter names (C is 'see', A is 'ay') differ from the sounds the letters usually make in words. isiZulu and Sesotho letters are usually called by their sound.
tags.teachingStrategy: Teach sounds first for reading; introduce names later for spelling aloud and forms.
